Correspondingly, the wet body mass of a newborn individual is approximately 3.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.2 grams], a modest size that scales predictably with the cubed ratio of neonatal to adult length. This initial mass is particularly low compared to many congeners, underscoring a life-history strategy that prioritizes early emergence over large offspring size. The relatively abbreviated incubation period, at these cool temperatures, allows neonates to take advantage of the late-summer prey abundance, primarily earthworms and soft-bodied invertebrates, before the onset of their first winter dormancy. Seasonal timing therefore plays a crucial role in determining juvenile survival rates.

Such energetic investment per offspring is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy.
